title: Chapter 21 — Of Parliamentary Eloquence In The United States
paragraphs: Among aristocratic nations all the members of the community are connected with and dependent on each other; the graduated scale of different ranks acts as a tie that keeps everyone in his proper place and the whole body in subordination. Something of the same kind always happens in the political assemblies of these nations. Parties naturally range themselves under certain leaders, whom they obey by a sort of instinct, which is only the result of habits contracted elsewhere. They carry the manners of general society into the lesser assemblage.

In democratic countries it often happens that a great number of citizens are tending toward the same point, but each moves there, or at least flatters himself that he moves, of his own accord. Accustomed to regulate his doings by personal impulse alone, he does not willingly submit to dictation from without. This taste and habit of independence accompany him into the councils of the nation. If he consents to connect himself with other men in the pursuit of the same purpose, at least he insists on remaining free to contribute to the common success in his own way. Hence, in democratic countries, parties are so impatient of control, and are never manageable except in moments of great public danger. Even then, the authority of leaders, which in such circumstances may be able to make men act or speak, hardly ever reaches the point of making them keep silent.

Among aristocratic nations, the members of political assemblies are also members of the aristocracy. Each of them enjoys an established rank in his own right, and the position he occupies in the assembly is often less important in his eyes than the one he fills in the country. This consoles him for playing no part in the discussion of public affairs, and restrains him from too eagerly attempting to play an insignificant one.

In America, it generally happens that a Representative only becomes somebody through his position in the Assembly. He is therefore perpetually haunted by a craving to acquire importance there, and he feels a petulant desire to be constantly obtruding his opinions on the House. His own vanity is not the only stimulant driving him on in this course — there is also the vanity of his constituents, and the continual necessity of propitiating them. Among aristocratic nations, a member of the legislature is rarely in strict dependence on his constituents. He is often a sort of unavoidable representative for them; sometimes they are themselves strictly dependent on him; and if in the end they reject him, he may easily get elected elsewhere, or, retiring from public life, he may still enjoy the pleasures of splendid idleness. In a democratic country like the United States, a Representative hardly ever has a lasting hold on the minds of his constituents. However small an electoral body may be, the fluctuations of democracy are constantly changing its aspect; it must therefore be courted unceasingly. He is never sure of his supporters, and if they forsake him he is left without a resource, for his natural position is not elevated enough for him to be easily known to those outside his immediate circle; and with the complete state of independence prevailing among the people, he cannot hope that his friends or the government will send him down to be returned by an electoral body unacquainted with him. The seeds of his fortune are therefore sown in his own neighborhood; from that nook of earth he must start, to raise himself to the command of a people and to influence the destinies of the world. Thus it is natural that in democratic countries the members of political assemblies think more of their constituents than of their party, while in aristocracies they think more of their party than of their constituents.

But what ought to be said to gratify constituents is not always what ought to be said to serve the party to which Representatives profess to belong. The general interest of a party frequently demands that its members should not speak on great questions they understand imperfectly; that they should speak only a little on those minor questions that impede the great ones; and lastly, and for the most part, that they should not speak at all. To keep silent is the most useful service an indifferent spokesman can render to the commonwealth. Constituents, however, do not think so. The population of a district sends a representative to take part in the government of a country because they entertain a very lofty notion of his merits. Since men appear greater in proportion to the littleness of the objects surrounding them, the opinion held of the delegate will be so much the higher as talents are more rare among his constituents. It will therefore frequently happen that the less constituents have to expect from their representative, the more they will anticipate from him; and however incompetent he may be, they will not fail to call upon him for signal exertions, corresponding to the rank they have conferred on him.

Besides regarding him as a legislator of the State, the electors also see their Representative as the natural patron of the constituency in the Legislature. They almost consider him the proxy of each of his supporters, and they flatter themselves that he will be no less zealous in defense of their private interests than of those of the country. Thus the electors are well assured beforehand that the Representative of their choice will be an orator, that he will speak often if he can, and that, if he is forced to refrain, he will at least strive to compress into his less frequent orations an inquiry into all the great questions of state, combined with a statement of all the petty grievances they have to complain of. So even if he is not able to come forward frequently, he should on each occasion prove what he is capable of; and instead of perpetually lavishing his powers, he should occasionally condense them in a small compass, so as to furnish a sort of complete and brilliant epitome of his constituents and of himself. On these terms they will vote for him at the next election. These conditions drive worthy men of humble abilities to despair, men who, knowing their own powers, would never voluntarily have come forward. But thus urged on, the Representative begins to speak, to the great alarm of his friends; and rushing imprudently into the midst of the most celebrated orators, he perplexes the debate and wearies the House.

All laws that tend to make the Representative more dependent on the elector not only affect the conduct of the legislators, as I have remarked elsewhere, but also their language. They exercise a simultaneous influence on affairs themselves and on the manner in which affairs are discussed.

There is hardly a member of Congress who can make up his mind to go home without having dispatched at least one speech to his constituents, or who will endure any interruption until he has introduced into his harangue whatever useful suggestions can be made touching the twenty-four States of which the Union is composed — and especially the district he represents. He therefore presents to the minds of his auditors a succession of great general truths (which he himself only understands and expresses confusedly), and of petty minutiae, which he is only too able to discover and point out. The consequence is that the debates of that great assembly are frequently vague and perplexed, and they seem to drag their slow length along rather than to advance toward any distinct object. Some such state of things will, I believe, always arise in the public assemblies of democracies.

Propitious circumstances and good laws might succeed in drawing to the legislature of a democratic people men far superior to those the Americans return to Congress; but nothing will ever prevent the men of slender abilities who sit there from obtruding themselves with complacency, and in every way, upon the public. The evil does not appear to me susceptible of entire cure, because it originates not only in the tactics of that assembly but in its constitution and in that of the country. The inhabitants of the United States seem themselves to consider the matter in this light, and they show their long experience of parliamentary life not by abstaining from making bad speeches, but by courageously submitting to hear them. They are resigned to it, as to an evil they know to be inevitable.

We have shown the petty side of political debates in democratic assemblies — let us now exhibit the more imposing one. The proceedings within the Parliament of England for the last one hundred and fifty years have never caused any great sensation outside that country; the opinions and feelings expressed by the speakers have never awakened much sympathy, even among the nations placed nearest to the great arena of British liberty. Europe, on the other hand, was stirred by the very first debates that took place in the small colonial assemblies of America at the time of the Revolution. This was attributable not only to particular and fortuitous circumstances, but to general and lasting causes. I can conceive of nothing more admirable or more powerful than a great orator debating on great questions of state in a democratic assembly. Since no particular class is ever represented there by men commissioned to defend its own interests, it is always to the whole nation, and in the name of the whole nation, that the orator speaks. This expands his thoughts and heightens his power of language. Since precedents have little weight there — since there are no longer any privileges attached to certain kinds of property, nor any rights inherent in certain bodies or certain individuals — the mind must have recourse to general truths drawn from human nature to resolve the particular question under discussion. Hence the political debates of a democratic people, however small it may be, have a degree of breadth that frequently makes them attractive to all mankind. All men are interested in them, because they treat of man, who is everywhere the same. Among the greatest aristocratic nations, by contrast, the most general questions are almost always argued on some particular grounds drawn from the practice of a particular time, or from the rights of a particular class — grounds that interest that class alone, or at most the people among whom that class happens to exist. It is to this, as much as to the greatness of the French people and the favorable disposition of the nations who listen to them, that we must attribute the great effect French political debates sometimes produce in the world. The orators of France frequently speak to mankind, even when they are addressing their countrymen alone.
